newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Richemont plans more TV investment.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Richemont plans more TV investment.

text.p: Swiss-based Compagnie Financiere Richemont AG plans more investments in pay television, but is waiting for prices to fall before making any big moves, managing director Johann Rupert said on Monday.

"We are in pay television...We are happy with our involvement, and as the cash flows build up in our Richemont group, we are looking to extend further investments in that area," he told Reuters Financial Television from South Africa.

Rupert was interviewed after Richemont reported operating profit for the six months to September 30 rose 31.7 percent to 466.2 million pounds from 354.1 million a year earlier, excluding exceptional items and goodwill amortisation.
Asked where the tobacco, luxury goods and television group might expand in future, he left the question open.

"If I knew, I wouldn't tell you. I think the markets are very very high, they are skittish. If I look at smart investors in many parts of the world, they are looking at building up some liquidity for the downturn that will inevitably follow.
"With the Dow and the FTSE both at record levels, I think we would be looking at preserving cash for a while," he added.
France's Canal Plus agreed in September to buy pay-television group NetHold BV from Richemont and MIH Holdings Ltd for $45 million cash and 6.1 million new Canal Plus shares.

Rupert said the deal, which created one of the world's largest pay TV companies with 8.5 million subscribers, was going to plan and that a definitive accord giving Richemont a 15 percent stake in Canal Plus was set to be signed on December 12.
The company has made clear the deal will have an impact on its earnings only in the next fiscal year.
Richemont's net sales grew 15 percent to 2,343.6 million pounds ($3.95 billion).
The company said in a statement it expected to maintain the group's profitability.
"We believe that the group's overall profitability for the current financial year as a whole will continue to reflect the trend seen in the first six months of the year," Richemont said.
But Rupert said Richemont was cautious about prospects for Rothmans International, the vehicle for its tobacco interests, whose hefty growth was being weighed on by the strong pound.
"We have seen quite a bit of buying-in ahead of the budget in the U.K. but things are going according to track and according to plan for the long-term business," he said.
"We are satisfied with the performance in the first six months, although in sterling terms obviously we are suffering," he said, adding sterling's rate would affect full-year results.

Rothmans operating profit as reported rose 51.9 percent in the half to 401.1 million sterling. This relected a 12.3 percent rise in underlying tobacco operating profit and the January merger with Rembrandt Group's tobacco business.

Rupert said production of luxury goods in hard-currency countries like Switzerland also posed a problem. Operating profit from the Vendome Luxury Group dipped 2.6 percent to 110.4 million sterling but was nearly steady in Swiss francs.

"Even though the Swiss franc may have weakened somewhat against sterling, the trend for the Swiss franc and the D-mark against third-party currencies has remained strong...As our costs are incurred in hard currencies for both the pens and the watches, again, we have a bit of currency problem," he said.
Richemont owns such famous brandnames as Cartier, Mont Blanc, Rothmans and Dunhill. It said Vendome sales and operating profits should rise in franc terms for the rest of the year.
Richemont shares were up 30 Swiss francs to 1,955 in late trading in Zurich, countering the lower overall trend.
